She has **persistently active, structurally progressive peripheral psoriatic arthritis despite upadacitinib**, with high disease activity (DAPSA ≈31), unequivocal Doppler-positive synovitis and bilateral Achilles enthesitis, and a new MCP erosion.  
This is a difficult-to-treat phenotype with objective inflammatory treatment failure—not pain amplification alone—although obesity, mechanical entheseal pain and concomitant fibromyalgia may contribute, and tenderness at the other entheseal sites does not itself establish active enthesitis.  
Review adherence, treatment interruptions, the adequacy and reasons for previous drug failures, and relevant comorbidities, particularly psoriasis burden, inflammatory bowel disease and uveitis, while evaluating fatigue for additional causes.  
**I would switch rather than continue upadacitinib unchanged**, favouring an untried IL-23 inhibitor such as guselkumab or risankizumab, subject to shared decision-making and local access; an alternative TNF inhibitor remains reasonable depending on why adalimumab failed and associated disease manifestations.  
Do not combine a biologic with upadacitinib; arrange appropriate infection screening and vaccination review, and consider targeted intra-articular corticosteroid injections as bridging treatment while avoiding injection into the Achilles tendons.  
Provide physiotherapy, weight-management and pain support alongside disease-modifying treatment, then reassess objectively within approximately 8–12 weeks, aiming for clear improvement by three months and remission or low disease activity by six months.

She has **persistently active, erosive psoriatic arthritis with high disease activity (DAPSA ≈31), objectively confirmed synovitis and Achilles enthesitis, and radiographic progression despite seven months of upadacitinib**.  
This is a difficult-to-treat, multidrug-exposed phenotype; obesity or concomitant pain amplification may contribute to symptoms, but neither explains the Doppler inflammation, swollen joints and new erosion, so her pain must not be dismissed as non-inflammatory.  
I would confirm adherence and adequate exposure to previous treatments, clarify primary versus secondary failures, and assess psoriasis, axial disease, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis and infection before selecting the next therapy.  
**Upadacitinib should be replaced rather than continued unchanged**: an IL-23p19 inhibitor such as guselkumab or risankizumab is a reasonable next mechanism for her peripheral arthritis and enthesitis, with an alternative TNF inhibitor also reasonable depending on why adalimumab failed and associated disease.  
After excluding infection, targeted intra-articular glucocorticoid injections could bridge symptomatic synovitis, alongside appropriate analgesia, physiotherapy and weight-management support; avoid injection into the Achilles tendon and do not combine a biologic with upadacitinib.  
Complete relevant infection screening and vaccination review, then reassess objectively within about three months using joint examination, CRP and a validated activity score, aiming for remission or low disease activity and further treatment adjustment if that target is not achieved.

She has **persistently active, erosive psoriatic arthritis despite multiple advanced therapies**, with high peripheral disease activity (DAPSA ≈31), objectively confirmed synovitis and Achilles enthesitis, and radiographic progression while taking upadacitinib.  
This is a difficult-to-treat, potentially treatment-refractory inflammatory phenotype: obesity and pain amplification may contribute to fatigue and tenderness, but cannot explain the Doppler inflammation, swollen joints and new erosion, and tenderness alone does not establish inflammation at every entheseal site.  
I would confirm adherence, adequacy and reasons for failure of previous treatments, exclude intercurrent infection, and assess psoriasis, axial disease, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis and relevant comorbidities before choosing the next agent.  
Given seven months of inadequate response with structural progression, I recommend **switching from upadacitinib rather than continuing unchanged or increasing its dose**, favouring an untried mechanism such as an IL-23 inhibitor (guselkumab or risankizumab) if peripheral arthritis/enthesitis predominates; an alternative TNF inhibitor remains reasonable depending on why adalimumab failed and associated disease.  
After appropriate infection screening and vaccination review, targeted intra-articular glucocorticoid injections for symptomatic swollen joints and a short NSAID course, if safe, can provide bridging relief, alongside physiotherapy, weight management and assessment of sleep, mood and other causes of fatigue; avoid injecting the Achilles tendon itself and do not overlap upadacitinib with a biologic.  
Reassess within approximately 8–12 weeks using swollen joints, CRP, DAPSA and domain-specific examination, aiming for substantial improvement by three months and remission or low disease activity by six months, with prompt further adjustment if objective inflammation persists.

This is **high-activity, treatment-refractory erosive psoriatic arthritis** (DAPSA approximately 31), with unequivocal Doppler-positive synovitis, inflammatory Achilles enthesitis and progressive structural damage; obesity or pain amplification cannot explain these findings alone.  
I would verify adherence and the adequacy/reasons for previous treatment failures, exclude intercurrent infection, and review psoriasis, axial symptoms, IBD and uveitis because these influence drug selection.  
After seven months without adequate control, I recommend **switching from upadacitinib to an untried mechanism**, preferably an IL-23p19 inhibitor such as guselkumab or risankizumab for this peripheral/entheseal phenotype, through shared decision-making with appropriate infection screening and vaccination review; do not combine it with upadacitinib.  
Ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injections into troublesome inflamed joints and/or a short NSAID course, if safe, can provide bridging relief, but avoid corticosteroid injections at the Achilles insertions.  
Reassess joint swelling, enthesitis, function, CRP and DAPSA in 8–12 weeks, seeking substantial improvement by three months and remission or low disease activity by six months, with further treatment adjustment if these targets are missed.  
Concurrently address weight, cardiovascular risk and physical conditioning, and assess sleep, mood and possible coexisting fibromyalgia as contributors to fatigue and pain **without allowing these to delay control of demonstrated inflammation**.

This is **high-activity, treatment-refractory inflammatory psoriatic arthritis** (DAPSA 31), with objectively confirmed synovitis, Doppler-positive Achilles enthesitis and radiographic progression over the past year despite multiple treatment mechanisms being tried.  
Obesity and coexisting pain amplification may contribute to fatigue and tenderness elsewhere, but they do not explain the swollen, warm joints, Doppler activity and new erosion, so this should not be managed as predominantly non-inflammatory pain.  
I would confirm adherence and adequate exposure to previous treatments, clarify primary versus secondary failures or intolerance, and review psoriasis, axial symptoms, IBD, uveitis and safety considerations before **switching from inadequately effective upadacitinib**.  
An **IL-23p19 inhibitor such as guselkumab or risankizumab** is a reasonable next mechanism for this peripheral arthritis/enthesitis phenotype; another TNF inhibitor remains an alternative depending on the adalimumab failure and comorbidities, but combining a biologic with upadacitinib or escalating beyond its approved PsA dose is not recommended.  
After appropriate infection screening and vaccination review, arrange the switch, with intra-articular glucocorticoid injections into selected inflamed joints and a short NSAID course if safe as bridging measures, alongside physiotherapy, weight management and assessment of other contributors to fatigue.  
Reassess swollen joints, CRP and a validated activity measure within **8–12 weeks**, targeting substantial improvement by three months and remission or low disease activity by six months, with specialist multidisciplinary review if objective inflammation persists.

This is **highly active, erosive, multi-domain PsA with a treatment-refractory inflammatory phenotype**: DAPSA 31 indicates high disease activity, ultrasound confirms synovitis and Achilles enthesitis, and the new erosion demonstrates interval structural progression—not simply persistent pain without inflammation.  
Obesity, mechanical entheseal pain or pain amplification may coexist, but cannot explain the swollen, warm, Doppler-positive joints; confirm adherence and the adequacy/reasons for previous treatment failures, and assess psoriasis, axial symptoms, IBD/uveitis and infection risk before selecting treatment.  
I would **switch from upadacitinib rather than continue it unchanged**, favouring an untried mechanism such as an IL-23p19 inhibitor—guselkumab or risankizumab—after appropriate safety screening and shared decision-making; another TNF inhibitor remains reasonable, particularly if adalimumab initially worked or active uveitis favours that class.  
Do not increase upadacitinib above its licensed PsA dose or combine it with a biologic; short-term NSAIDs and/or selected intra-articular glucocorticoid injections can bridge the switch if safe, avoiding intratendinous Achilles injections.  
Address weight, graded activity and physiotherapy alongside fatigue contributors such as anaemia, sleep apnoea, poor sleep and depression, without allowing these measures to delay control of inflammation.  
Reassess swollen joints, CRP, enthesitis and DAPSA within **8–12 weeks**, seeking substantial improvement by three months and remission or low disease activity by six months, with earlier reconsideration for deterioration or further damage.

He has **low clinical disease activity, but not remission, with ongoing inflammatory activity and structural progression despite adalimumab**; feeling well and a DAPSA of 7.6 do not establish adequate disease control when new erosions are developing.  
I would review the serial radiographs to confirm genuine progression and reassess peripheral joints, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin/nails and axial symptoms, noting that Doppler-positive synovitis supports residual inflammation.  
After confirming progression, I would discuss the risk of irreversible damage and recommend **modifying disease-modifying treatment rather than continuing adalimumab unchanged**, using shared decision-making.  
A switch to another biologic is appropriate—often an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor, selected according to psoriasis severity, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis and other comorbidities—although another TNF inhibitor remains reasonable, particularly after secondary loss of response.  
An injection into the persistently swollen MCP may help locally but would not substitute for systemic treatment adjustment given multisite inflammation and new erosions.  
I would reassess clinically within approximately 3 months, aiming preferably for remission, and arrange follow-up structural imaging around 12 months, using ultrasound selectively rather than escalating solely to eliminate every Doppler signal.

This is **clinically low disease activity but inadequately controlled psoriatic arthritis**, with ongoing objective synovitis and structural progression despite adalimumab; the reassuring DAPSA and preserved function do not negate new erosions.  
I would confirm that the radiographs are technically comparable and the erosions genuinely new, review the full disease phenotype and adalimumab dosing, and discuss the risk of irreversible damage with him.  
If progression is confirmed, I would recommend **changing disease-modifying therapy rather than continuing unchanged**, because this is radiographic progression supported by clinical swelling and Doppler inflammation—not ultrasound abnormalities alone.  
After adequate TNF-inhibitor exposure, switching to an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor is reasonable, although another TNF inhibitor remains an option, with selection guided by psoriasis, axial disease, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis, safety, and patient preference.  
A local glucocorticoid injection could help the persistently swollen MCP as an adjunct, but would not substitute for addressing systemic treatment failure.  
I would reassess clinically and with CRP in approximately three months, aiming for remission if feasible, use ultrasound selectively to clarify residual inflammation rather than mandate imaging remission, and repeat radiographs in about 12 months to assess structural stability.

He has **low clinical disease activity, but not remission, with ongoing inflammatory synovitis and radiographic progression despite adalimumab**; feeling well and a low DAPSA do not establish adequate disease control when new structural damage is occurring.  
I would review the paired radiographs to confirm genuine new erosions, verify dosing and administration, and reassess all PsA domains and relevant comorbidities; ultrasound supports residual inflammation but should not alone dictate escalation.  
If progression is confirmed, I would explain the discordance and recommend **changing disease-modifying treatment rather than continuing adalimumab unchanged**, through shared decision-making aimed at preventing further irreversible damage.  
Switching to another biologic—often an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway inhibitor, selected according to psoriasis, axial disease, IBD, uveitis, and patient preference—is reasonable, although another TNF inhibitor remains an option, particularly after a previous good response; reactive adalimumab level/antibody testing may help where available but is not routinely required.  
A local glucocorticoid injection can help the persistently swollen MCP as an adjunct, but would not adequately address inflammation at multiple sites or substitute for systemic treatment modification.  
I would reassess clinical response within approximately three months, aim for remission or sustained low disease activity **without further structural progression**, and repeat radiographs at about 12 months, using targeted ultrasound when it would clarify management.

Despite DAPSA-defined low disease activity, this is **active, structurally progressive PsA with an inadequate response to adalimumab**: new erosions, residual joint swelling and Doppler-positive synovitis outweigh reassurance from the composite score alone.  
I would confirm progression on comparable radiographs, reassess all PsA domains, and explain that irreversible damage can accumulate despite feeling well.  
Through shared decision-making, I would **change systemic therapy rather than continue adalimumab unchanged**, generally switching to another bDMARD—an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor, or another TNF inhibitor—selected according to prior response, psoriasis, axial disease, IBD/uveitis and patient preference.  
Reactive adalimumab trough and antidrug-antibody testing, where available and actionable, may help distinguish underexposure or immunogenicity from mechanistic failure, but is not mandatory.  
The aim is clinical remission where feasible and prevention of further damage; ultrasound supports the assessment but ultrasound remission alone is not an established treatment target.  
I would reassess clinically and biochemically within 8–12 weeks, use ultrasound selectively to clarify residual inflammation, and repeat radiographs at approximately 12 months to check structural stability.

This is **low clinical disease activity but inadequate disease control**: new erosions, a swollen MCP, and Doppler-positive synovitis indicate ongoing inflammation with structural progression despite acceptable symptoms.  
I would confirm that the erosions are genuinely new on comparable radiographs, review adalimumab dosing and the other PsA domains, and explain the risk of irreversible damage despite feeling well.  
With progression confirmed, I would recommend **changing systemic therapy through shared decision-making**, rather than continuing adalimumab unchanged because DAPSA is low—for example, switching to an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor selected according to psoriasis, axial involvement, IBD/uveitis, and safety considerations.  
Another TNF inhibitor is also reasonable, particularly with suspected secondary loss of response; reactive adalimumab trough/antidrug-antibody testing may help guide this choice where available, but is not mandatory.

I would reassess joints, symptoms, and CRP within approximately 3 months, aiming for remission and prevention of further damage, and repeat radiographs at about 12 months.

This is **inadequately controlled, structurally progressive psoriatic arthritis despite low clinical disease activity**: DAPSA 7.6 is not remission, and new erosions plus Doppler-positive synovitis indicate residual inflammation and ongoing joint damage on adalimumab.  
I would review comparable radiographs to confirm genuine progression, reassess all PsA domains, and explain that feeling well does not necessarily mean the joints are protected.  
If progression is confirmed, I would recommend **changing disease-modifying treatment through shared decision-making**, rather than continuing adalimumab unchanged or tapering, aiming for clinical remission and prevention of further damage.  
Switching to an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor is reasonable, while another TNF inhibitor remains an option; selection should reflect skin and axial involvement, IBD or uveitis, comorbidities, and patient preferences.  
Reactive adalimumab trough-level and anti-drug-antibody testing, where available, may help distinguish inadequate drug exposure from failure of the mechanism, but is not mandatory before changing treatment.  
I would reassess joints, function, patient-reported outcomes, and CRP within 8–12 weeks, use ultrasound selectively to clarify residual inflammation rather than pursue imaging remission alone, and repeat radiographs at approximately 12 months to assess further progression.

The most likely diagnosis is **active axial spondyloarthritis**, supported by inflammatory back pain, HLA-B27 positivity, elevated inflammatory markers, and extensive sacroiliac inflammation with structural lesions; radiographic versus non-radiographic status requires assessment of plain-film sacroiliitis, and these findings alone do not establish psoriatic arthritis.  
She also meets symptom-score thresholds for **coexisting fibromyalgia**, provided pain involves at least four of five body regions and symptoms have persisted for at least three months; obesity and scoliosis may contribute additional mechanical pain but do not adequately explain the inflammatory findings.  
Given persistently high disease activity and objective inflammation despite two adequate NSAID trials, I recommend **starting a biologic—either a TNF inhibitor or an IL-17 inhibitor—through shared decision-making**, rather than further NSAID cycling or methotrexate for isolated axial disease.  
Check for psoriasis, uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease to guide selection: a monoclonal TNF inhibitor is preferred with recurrent uveitis or active inflammatory bowel disease, whereas substantial psoriasis may favour IL-17 inhibition, which should be avoided in active inflammatory bowel disease.  
Before treatment, screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C, obtain baseline safety blood tests, review vaccinations, infection risks and pregnancy plans, and arrange physiotherapy-led exercise, weight-management support, and parallel fibromyalgia care addressing sleep, graded activity and psychological strategies.  
Reassess after approximately 12–16 weeks using ASDAS-CRP, inflammatory markers, function and clinical findings, recognising that fibromyalgia can inflate symptom-based scores and that persistent widespread pain alone should not trigger biologic escalation.

Her widespread pain, fatigue and unrefreshing sleep meet the WPI/symptom-severity thresholds for fibromyalgia, provided generalized pain distribution and symptom duration are confirmed; this can inflate patient-reported disease activity but does not negate the objective inflammation.  
Plain pelvic radiographs can distinguish radiographic from non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, while history and examination should assess psoriasis, peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease—there is insufficient information to label this psoriatic arthritis specifically.  
Given **very high disease activity (ASDAS-CRP 3.6), objective inflammation and failure of two adequate NSAID trials**, I recommend starting a biologic, usually a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor, after tuberculosis/hepatitis screening, vaccination review and discussion of pregnancy plans and other contraindications.  
Choose a monoclonal TNF inhibitor if recurrent uveitis or active inflammatory bowel disease is present, whereas significant psoriasis may favour an IL-17 inhibitor; conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate are not effective for purely axial disease.  
Concurrently provide tailored physiotherapy, graded aerobic and strengthening exercise, weight-management support and fibromyalgia-focused sleep and pain care, reassessing inflammatory response after approximately 12–16 weeks without escalating immunosuppression solely for persistent widespread pain.

PsAID-12 of 5.5 indicates an unacceptable patient-reported disease impact (acceptable state generally ≤4), although it is not itself a measure of inflammation; strictly, the supplied components yield DAPSA 4.2 after converting CRP to mg/dL, just above the remission threshold of ≤4.

Agree on functional and symptom targets, provide occupational/hand-therapy support, and reassess within about 8–12 weeks using examination, patient-reported impact and targeted ultrasound where helpful, rather than escalating solely to eliminate every Doppler signal.

Occupational/hand therapy and temporary symptom relief can support him meanwhile, with reassessment in about 8–12 weeks using symptoms, function, examination, PsAID and, where useful, repeat ultrasound rather than DAPSA alone.
